newsitem.title: USA: Refco forecasts '97 US corn area at 80 mln acres.
newsitem.headline: Refco forecasts '97 US corn area at 80 mln acres.

text.p: Refco Global Research said Monday it projected U.S. corn planted area in 1997 at 80.0 million acres, soybean area at 66.0 million acres and wheat area at 69.3 million acres.
Last year U.S. corn planted area totalled 79.49 million, soybean area was 64.21 million and wheat area was 75.64 million, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

In remarks prepared for a series of outlook seminars this week, analyst Rich Feltes said using trend yields, these areas suggested 1997/98 carryover stocks of 1.5 billion bushels for corn, 215 million for soybeans and 643 million for wheat.
Earlier this month USDA projected 1996/97 corn ending stocks of 959 million bushels, soybeans at 140 million and wheat at 474 million.

"The 1997 U.S. corn yield must decline five percent below trend - 6.5 bushels per acre or more - before 97/98 U.S. corn stocks would fall below 96/97 corn stocks," Feltes said, noting this had happened in three of the last eight years.
He said a 500-million-bushel gain suggested a low for December corn of $2.40 a bushel on the Chicago Board of Trade while a 1.0-billion-gain suggested a $2.20 a bushel low.
USDA is due to issue forecasts for U.S. grain and oilseed plantings this year on March 31.
- Refco forecast a two-million-tonne rise in Chinese oilseed production this year, half of which would be soybeans.
- Strong growth in Chinese poultry production suggested imports of soymeal could swell to more than 4.0 million tonnes in '97/98 versus 3.3 million in '96/97.

- May soybeans are poised to exceed $9.00 a bushel if the weekly pace of export sales and crush does not retreat quickly from the recent 17.1-million-bushel- and 30-million-bushel-a -week pace, respectively.
- Meal will probably maintain soy product leadership as tax changes in the world's largest soymeal exporter - Brazil - push more meal business to the U.S.

- Pipeline supplies of U.S. soybeans are better stocked today than corn and wheat were a year ago. The current rally in beans is driven more by a shortfall in offshore oilseed production than by a shortage of U.S. soybeans.
- Indicators suggested favorable 1997 U.S. crop weather. Subsoil moisture was above average and there was no history of low row crop yields in years of heavy late winter moisture.
